papers.title: Mathematics of Herding
papers.abstract: A herd of animals often follows a leader who sets the direction of travel. The leader sometimes turns unexpectedly and the followers reshuffle. Yet the herd regroups itself and stays coherent. Our work aims to understand the herding behavior mathematically. We construct a minimal discrete-time nonequilibrium dynamical system with one-way coupling, and the minimal structure allows an exact analysis. Take the location of each follower in the frame of the leader. The recorded locations form a distribution. The limit of the distribution is the asymptotic spatial measure, whose geometric representation we study. The dynamics of the herd have an exact operator representation with two factors, the operator of a fixed leader-follower pair and the operator of the interaction rules, which reshuffle the pairs. We show that the influence of the leader passes through some follower more than once. As a result, two followers can have reciprocal influence, despite the one-way coupling.

papers.title: Fate of Arnold tongues and canards in Mobius systems with noise
papers.abstract: We consider a class of noisy dynamical systems on the two-dimensional torus whose phase evolution is governed by Mobius transformations. In the deterministic limit, these systems favor phase-locking that is described by the band-gap structure of an associated Schrodinger equation with a periodic potential. We use the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin method to characterize this structure in the slow-fast limit. Then we show that large-deviation theory describes fluctuations of the finite-time rotation number, whereas weak-noise escape actions determine the exponential scale of rare phase slips. These estimates provide quantitative criteria for metastable phase-locking and melting of Arnold tongues over a prescribed observation time. We derive sufficient conditions for stochastic trajectories to follow prescribed canard segments. With controlled entrance errors, exponential amplification of fluctuations along repelling branches leads to an exponentially small sufficient noise scale for canard persistence in the slow-forcing limit.

papers.title: Trajectory arclength reveals chaos
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the time-averaged phase space arclength of a trajectory, expressed through a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, as a trajectory-based diagnostic for distinguishing regular and chaotic dynamics. The proposed indicator, $\Omega$, is computed by integrating the equations of motion together with a single scalar arclength-accumulation equation and therefore does not require variational equations, neighboring trajectories, or spatial derivatives of a Lagrangian descriptor field. Using Birkhoff's ergodic theorem together with estimates for quasiperiodic motion and correlation-based arguments for chaotic ergodic dynamics, we show that regular and chaotic trajectories exhibit different finite-time behavior despite the convergence of $\Omega$ in both regimes. For quasiperiodic trajectories with Diophantine frequency vectors, deviations from the limiting average decay as $\mathcal{O}(\tau^{-1})$, whereas sufficiently mixing chaotic dynamics exhibit root-mean-square fluctuations of order $\tau^{-1/2}$ under suitable correlation assumptions. This difference in finite-time convergence and fluctuation scaling provides the theoretical basis for using $\Omega$ to discriminate between the two dynamical regimes. We validate the proposed approach in the H\'enon--Heiles and Fermi--Pasta--Ulam systems, comparing the resulting classification of initial conditions with SALI as a reference chaos indicator. The results support $\Omega$ as a complementary single-trajectory diagnostic for chaos detection and as a practical source of scalar features for the analysis of trajectory ensembles, particularly in settings involving large numbers of trajectories or high-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Shearless and periodic attractors in the dissipative Labyrinthic map
papers.abstract: The Labyrinthic map is a two-dimensional area-preserving map that features a robust transport barrier known as the shearless curve. In this study, we explore a dissipative version of this map,examining how dissipation affects the shearless curve and leads to the emergence of quasi-periodic or chaotic attractors, referred to as shearless attractors. We present a route to chaos of the shearless attractor known as the Curry-Yorke route. To investigate the multi-stability of the system, we employ basin entropy and boundary basin entropy analyses to characterize diverse scenarios. Additionally, we numerically investigate the dynamic periodic structures known as "shrimps" and "Arnold tongues" by varying the parameters of the system.

papers.title: Reduced Arc-Weight Heterogeneity for Master Stability Analysis of Directed Networks
papers.abstract: Master stability analysis can be applied to directed networks even when their Laplacian matrices are not diagonalizable. Nevertheless, a diagonalizable Laplacian is easier to analyse because the perturbations governing synchronization separate into independent modes. This paper asks how many different positive coupling strengths are needed to obtain this simplification without adding or removing any directed connections. We first give an elementary construction showing that suitable positive weights exist for every weakly connected directed network and explain its relationship to stronger genericity results in the literature. We then introduce a measure of the smallest number of distinct coupling strengths required for diagonalizability. If a common coupling strength already produces a diagonalizable Laplacian, only one value is needed. For directed acyclic networks, we give a constructive upper bound based on the length of the longest directed path from a source. This bound is exact for rooted outward directed trees. Consequently, an outward star requires only one coupling value, whereas a directed path requires a different value on every arc. These results reduce coupling heterogeneity while retaining the simpler modal form of master stability analysis. Diagonalizability is treated as an analytical convenience, not as a sufficient condition for synchronization.

papers.title: An active Lorentz gas: walking droplets in periodic media
papers.abstract: The Lorentz gas is a paradigmatic model in dynamical systems theory for understanding the origin of nonequilibrium transport in terms of microscopic deterministic chaos. In the periodic setting, a point particle scatters elastically off disks arranged on a two-dimensional lattice. Here we replace the disks by smooth potentials and the particle by the widely studied walking droplet, which propels itself on a vertically vibrating fluid. In the low-memory limit, this droplet reduces to a particle with nonlinear active friction. We call this system an active Lorentz gas. Using extensive numerical simulations, we analyze how dissipation generated by the active deterministic dynamics alters the phase-space structure of the corresponding conservative Lorentz gas. We find that islands of stability collapse into attracting and repelling sets. To characterize these structures, we introduce an energy-variance filtering method that distinguishes localized periodic, quasi-ballistic periodic, and chaotic trajectories, enabling the construction of bifurcation diagrams in a non-conservative setting. We identify parameter regimes exhibiting strong bifurcation cascades, anomalous diffusion, and significant phase-space contraction. Our results establish the active Lorentz gas as a rich framework for studying transport in dissipative dynamical systems and provide a bridge between active matter and classical models of chaotic transport, with potential implications for hydrodynamic quantum analogs in periodic media.
